title: Yudha Kanda: The Great War of Liberation
body:
Yudha Kanda: The Great War of Liberation

39. Ravana-virachita-samara-vijaya Rama
40. Vibhishana-sharanagata-raja-prada Rama
41. Setu-bandhana-karana Rama
42. Kumbhakarna-prana-harana-karana Rama
43. Indrajit-sira-cchedana-karana-shoka-shamana Rama
44. Ravana-sira-cchedana-karana Rama

The Bridge of Faith and the Squirrels' Contribution

Plunged into action by Hanuman's news, Rama's army marched to the southern sea. The monkey architects Nala and Nila constructed a miraculous bridge of floating stones, and the entire army crossed to the shores of Lanka. In Lanka, Ravana's brother Vibhishana pleaded with him to return Sita and seek peace, but Ravana kicked him out of the palace in a fury. Vibhishana flew across the sea to seek refuge in Rama's camp.
The monkey leaders were deeply suspicious. Was he a spy sent to destroy them? But Rama made a historic declaration of unconditional grace: 'It is my eternal vow that if any living being, even if it is Ravana himself, approaches me seeking refuge with a sincere heart, saying "I am yours," I will grant them protection and security from all fear. Bring him forward.' This famous declaration of sharanagati remains a cornerstone of the epic's spiritual message, showing us that divine compassion knows no boundaries of race or lineage.
During the construction of the bridge, a beautiful and touching incident occurred, as celebrated in popular lore. As the massive monkeys were carrying colossal rocks and uprooted mountains to drop into the ocean, a tiny squirrel saw their efforts. Desiring to help, the squirrel rolled in the wet sand, ran to the bridge, and shook the grains of sand from its fur into the crevices between the stones. A monkey commander, annoyed, was about to brush the tiny creature aside. But Rama gently scooped the squirrel into his hands, stroking its back, and said: 'Look at this small being. The rocks of the monkeys are mighty, but the squirrel's contribution, offered with its full strength and a pure heart, is no less precious in my eyes.' This beautiful episode teaches us that the value of our service is not measured by its physical scale, but by the love and devotion with which it is offered.

The Clash of Titans and the Sanjivani Mountain

A devastating war commenced. The armies clashed, and the sky was darkened by missiles. Indrajit, Ravana's son, used his deceptive magical arts, striking Lakshmana with the deadly Shakti weapon, leaving him unconscious on the battlefield, poised to die at the following sunrise. To save his brother, Hanuman was sent to the Himalayan Dronagiri mountain to fetch the life-giving Sanjivani herb. Unable to identify the correct plant, Hanuman lifted the entire mountain and flew back across the sky, delivering it in time to revive Lakshmana.
Following Lakshmana's recovery, the giant Kumbhakarna was awakened from his deep slumber. He reproached Ravana for his sinful abduction of Sita but entered the battle out of deep loyalty to his brother, meeting his end at the hands of Rama. Indrajit, too, performed a secret, powerful sacrifice at Nikumbhila to become invincible, but Lakshmana, guided by Vibhishana, interrupted the ritual and slew him in a fierce, spectacular combat, breaking the backbone of Lanka's defense.

The Slaying of the Ten-Headed King and the Agni Pariksha

Furious and desperate, Ravana entered the battlefield himself. A spectacular, earth-shaking duel unfolded between Rama and Ravana. Rama cut off Ravana's heads, but due to a vessel of amrita—the nectar of immortality—stored in his stomach, they regenerated instantly. Guided by Vibhishana's advice and invoking the supreme Brahmastra, Rama fired the great arrow that pierced Ravana's chest, evaporated the amrita, and brought the mighty demon king down. Mandodari, weeping over his body, realised that Rama was none other than Lord Vishnu himself, and that her husband had brought about his own destruction through his sinful desires.
Following the victory, Sita was brought before Rama in beautiful garments. But even as she approached with tears of joy, Rama's countenance remained cold, and he looked down, refusing to meet her eyes: 'I fought this war to avenge the insult to my family, but I cannot take back a wife who has lived for a year in the house of another man.' At this sudden turn, the entire assembly was shocked. Sita, with supreme dignity, turned to Lakshmana and asked him to build a pyre: 'If my heart has never wavered from my husband, let the fire protect me.' She walked into the raging flames, and Agni, the lord of fire, rose from the pyre holding her completely unharmed, attesting to her absolute purity. Rama embraced her, explaining: 'I never doubted your purity for a second. But I had to perform this public trial so that the citizens of the world would accept and honor you as their queen.'
The long exile completed, Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana boarded the divine Pushpaka Vimanam to return to Ayodhya. As the celestial aircraft sailed through the sky, Rama pointed out the major landmarks to Sita, describing their journey in reverse: the massive bridge constructed by Nala and Nila, the sacred shores of Rameswaram, the Mount Rishyamukha where they met Sugriva, the beautiful Pampa Lake, the cottage at Panchavati, the hermitage of Sage Agastya, and the quiet woods of Chitrakoota. This beautiful overview allowed them to reflect on their long, painful journey, transforming their past sufferings into a golden thread of shared memories and ultimate triumph. They arrived in Ayodhya to find the city illuminated by millions of clay lamps, celebrating their return and the grand coronation of Rama as king.
